name: Montesquieu
role: French political philosopher and jurist, author of The Spirit of Laws (1748)
summary: Montesquieu defended moderate government under law, with power divided among separate bodies and a hereditary nobility as an intermediate power in monarchy. He treated laws as relative to climate, customs and the nature of each government, while holding that justice precedes positive law.

tax-the-wealthy.rationale: Book XIII ch. 7 calls the Athenian scheme fair, in which necessities were untaxed and superfluous wealth taxed more heavily than the useful, though it did not follow property exactly.

property-fundamental.rationale: Book XXVI ch. 15 lays down the maxim that when the public good is in question it is never to the public's advantage to deprive an individual of property, or retrench the least part of it by law; the public good consists in everyone's property being invariably preserved.

preserve-national-culture.rationale: Book XIX ch. 4-6 and 14 argue that a legislator should be attentive lest the general spirit of a nation (its manners and customs) be changed, that not everything should be corrected, and that laws should not be used to alter customs.

direct-votes.rationale: Book XI ch. 6: the people collectively are extremely unfit to discuss public affairs; their share should be choosing representatives who make the laws, and the ancient republics erred in letting the people act directly.

laws-from-scripture.rationale: Book XXVI ch. 2 says we ought not to decide by divine laws what should be decided by human laws, because the two differ in origin, object and nature.

territorial-expansion.rationale: Book X ch. 2 derives the right of war from necessity and strict justice and condemns wars on principles of glory, convenience and utility, which cuts against expanding because a nation is strong.

universal-morality.rationale: Book I ch. 1 holds there are relations of justice antecedent to positive law, so that things are not just merely because laws command them.

avoid-deficit-stimulus.rationale: Book XXII ch. 17 rejects the view that a state gains by owing debts to itself, listing its harms (interest drained abroad, taxes hurting manufactures) and saying he knows of no advantages.

ban-interest.rationale: Book XXII ch. 19 says lending without interest is only a counsel of religion, not civil law, that trade needs a price on money, and that prohibition, as in Mahometan countries, raises usury.

initiating-force-wrong.rationale: Book X ch. 2 states that a state's right of natural defence sometimes carries the necessity of attacking first, when another nation's continued peace would let it destroy her.

freedom-as-non-domination.rationale: Book XI ch. 3 and 6: political liberty is tranquillity of mind from the opinion of one's safety, so the government must be so constituted that one man need not be afraid of another; arbitrary power in a single person destroys it.

separated-powers.rationale: Book XI ch. 6: there is no liberty when legislative and executive power sit in one person or body, nor when judging is joined to either; he builds the English constitution on checks among the three.

emergency-suspend-protections.rationale: Book XI ch. 6: if the state is in danger from a conspiracy or foreign correspondence, the legislature may authorise the executive for a short, limited time to imprison suspected persons.

pool-sovereignty.rationale: Book IX ch. 1 recommends the confederate republic, in which several small states agree to join a larger body, as the way to combine internal liberty with external strength, and says the confederates keep their sovereignty.

head-commands-forces.rationale: Book XI ch. 6: once an army exists it should depend on the executive power, which belongs in the hands of a monarch, while the legislature votes the army annually and may disband it.

death-penalty.rationale: Book XII ch. 4 says a man who deprives or attempts to deprive another of life deserves death, calling it the remedy of a sick society.

sacred-ruler.rationale: Book XI ch. 6 says the person of the executive monarch should be sacred, meaning not answerable to the legislature, while his ministers can be punished.

character-from-environment.rationale: Book XIV makes the temper and passions of peoples depend on climate, and Book XIX ch. 4 lists climate, religion, laws, government maxims, precedents, morals and customs as what forms a nation's general spirit.

sovereign-above-law.rationale: Book II ch. 1-4 defines monarchy as rule by fixed laws and despotism as rule by caprice, which counts against a ruler above the law; Book XI ch. 6 puts the monarch's person beyond trial by the legislature, which counts for it.

mixed-constitution.rationale: Book XI ch. 6 sets out a constitution with a hereditary nobility and elected representatives sharing legislation under a monarch; he adds that this extreme of liberty is not the only good form and that mediums beat extremes.

land-redistribution.rationale: Book XXVI ch. 15 endorses Cicero's view that agrarian laws were unjust, because the community exists for each to keep his property, and bars taking property by law or political regulation for the public good.

apostasy-punishable.rationale: Book XXV ch. 12 says penal laws ought to be avoided in respect to religion and that they have only destroyed.

abolish-hereditary-privilege.rationale: Book II ch. 4 holds that no nobility means no monarchy and that abolishing the privileges of the lords leads to a popular or despotic state; Book XI ch. 6 says the body of nobles ought to be hereditary.

budget-needs-parliament.rationale: Book XI ch. 6: if the executive raised public money without the legislature's consent liberty would end, and the legislature should vote the subsidies from year to year, not for ever.

pronatalist-incentives.rationale: Book XXIII ch. 26-27 holds Europe needs laws favouring propagation and recommends general rewards, like the Romans', rather than only pensions for very large families.

notes: Sources are the Nugent/Prichard English text of The Spirit of Laws (Books I, II, IX, X-XIV, XIX, XX, XXII, XXIII, XXV, XXVI). Searched themes: government and constitution (XI), economy (taxes, interest, debt, property, commerce, population), religion, war, punishment, liberty and morality. Not read: Books III-IX, XV-XVIII, XXI, XXIV, XXVII-XXXI, the Persian Letters and the Considerations on the Romans. Most statements are about modern topics he never addressed and stay null.
